title: O living flame (John of the Cross)
hookLine: the first stanza of the Living Flame of Love
tomorrow: why would a man tell his own life story without saying i?

cards: The power's out. Someone digs a candle out of the kitchen drawer, and the whole table goes quiet, faces lit from below. The youngest leans in close and starts whispering to the flame, as if it might answer.
Nobody laughs. A Spanish friar named John of the Cross, Teresa's friend and fellow Carmelite, wrote a short poem that does the same thing. It doesn't describe a fire.
It talks to one: Oh llama de amor viva. O living flame of love. And what it asks that flame to do is not what you'd expect.

teach.b: First, who he's talking to. The poem speaks to the flame directly, and in his commentary John says this flame is the Holy Spirit. Living, not a fire lit once and slowly burning down.

The flame wounds, the stanza says, but tenderly, in the soul's deepest center. A tender wound sounds like a contradiction, and John means it to: the love goes all the way in, and it doesn't harm. Third, the change.
The flame, the poem says, is no longer hard to bear. Once it was. Earlier on this path, John's log in the fire hissed and blackened before it caught.
Here, the log has caught. Fourth, the request, and this is the surprise from the candle. You'd expect a soul to say: go easy, burn gently.
Instead it says, finish now, if you will, and tear the veil of this sweet encounter.

In John's reading, the veil is the thin thing still standing between the soul and God. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: John later went back and wrote a long commentary on this short poem, line by line.
A few lines of fire, and he needed a book to say what was inside them.

how: Some Catholic readers pray with John of the Cross's poems a stanza at a time, sometimes reading his own commentary on each line alongside, and some keep a candle lit while they read.

o: a candle lit for the dead on a saint's feast day
a punishing fire that burns away a soul's sins
love as a fire you speak to, asking it to finish

games.q: inside the first stanza — tap the pairs.
p: still between the soul and God

s: John's poem describes a fire from a safe distance
it speaks straight to the flame: O living flame of love.
the fire in the poem is a punishment
it wounds tenderly, at the soul's deepest center, and is no longer hard to bear.
in his commentary John says the flame is the Holy Spirit
the living flame of love, burning in the soul.

games.q: your friend is writing a song for her grandmother and keeps sanding down the chorus so nobody cries. what would John's poem ask of it?
o: let it burn all the way; a tender wound isn't harm.
sand it down; a feeling that strong only hurts people.
drop the song; fire like that belongs to saints only.
games.why: the soul in John's poem doesn't ask the flame to go easy. it calls the wound tender and says: finish now, tear the veil.

practice: If you can, light a candle or a small lamp, and keep your eyes on the flame. Let the first line move slowly with your breath: O living flame of love.
If you pray, you can speak it to God; if not, simply watch how a flame stays alive by moving.

wordCard.voice: O living flame. John's words spoken straight to God's love, a fire that wounds tenderly and is asked to finish its work. Today's word.

orig.note: Spanish, not Latin: 'living flame of love', the opening of John's poem.

carryVoice: Your line: o living flame. A fire you talk to, not only one you watch. Until tomorrow.
